summary: A modular monolith build: React SPA on the frontend, Go for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on Fly.io for about $1,190-2,817 a month. It plans for GDPR, builds on the team's Go, pushes live updates, and ships as one deployable that a team of 5 can build in 12 weeks.

frontend.justification: React SPA (Vite) is the frontend for a Realtime chat / collaboration / multiplayer project with about 10,000 daily users (~521 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 5 in 12 weeks. Search visibility is marked not needed (behind login), so rendering in the browser is acceptable, and it scores 5.0/5 for rich, app-like interaction. Next.js (React) is within 0.7 points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); the tie went to React SPA (Vite) on lower vendor lock-in (5 vs 6, summed lock-in).

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.7 points lower; either is defensible. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), learning curve (4.0 vs 3.0); Next.js (React) is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) takes a penalty: No search visibility needed: server rendering adds a Node.js server for pages that React SPA (Vite) serves as static files.

tradeoffs: Client-side rendering: the first screen waits for the JavaScript bundle to download and run
Routing, data fetching and state are your own architecture decisions

backend.justification: Go (net/http, chi or Gin) serves the API at about 521 requests/s at peak (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once)) for a team of 5. The team lists Go, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 4.5/5). It runs as a long-running Go service, so background jobs, WebSockets and database connection pools live in one deployable process. Realtime is core, and it scores 4.0/5 on realtime fit. It leads the runner-up, Elixir + Phoenix, by 3.1 points (out of 100 on the whole-stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. Go (net/http, chi or Gin) is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 2.0); Elixir + Phoenix is stronger on realtime fit (5.0 vs 4.0), development speed (4.0 vs 3.0); Elixir + Phoenix takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Elixir or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 5.1 points. Go (net/http, chi or Gin) is stronger on performance / latency (5.0 vs 3.0), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); Node.js + Express is stronger on development speed (4.0 vs 3.0), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0). 1.0 of the 5.1 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Tiny static binaries give near-instant cold starts on scale-to-zero platforms.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 11.0 points. Go (net/http, chi or Gin) is stronger on realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 3.0); Python + Django is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 3.0), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0); Python + Django takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Python or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn. 1.0 of the 11.0 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Tiny static binaries give near-instant cold starts on scale-to-zero platforms.

tradeoffs: More code for CRUD than Rails/Django

database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 200 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. The workload is write-heavy, and its write scaling scores 3/5. Its share of the estimated bill is $600-$1,244 a month, against a total budget of $1,500 a month. It leads the runner-up, Microsoft SQL Server, by 2.2 points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.2 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0), portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 3.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.2 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0); MySQL takes a penalty: Customers share one database and in MySQL privileges stop at table and column level, so the tenant filter lives in every application query.

tradeoffs: Single-writer primary: write scale-out needs sharding (Citus) or Aurora Limitless
Connection-per-process model needs PgBouncer/RDS Proxy under serverless

hosting.justification: Fly.io hosts the stack for users in Europe at a 99.9% availability target. It runs the Go API as long-running processes with WebSockets, sized for ~521 requests/s at peak. Its share of the estimated bill is $375-$845 a month, against a total budget of $1,500 a month. It leads the runner-up, Google Cloud Run, by 3.1 points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. Fly.io is stronger on realtime fit (5.0 vs 3.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 4.0); Google Cloud Run is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0). 1.0 of the 3.1 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Anycast + multi-region VMs keep websocket round-trips short for global users.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 10.9 points. Fly.io is stronger on realtime fit (5.0 vs 2.0), portability (low lock-in) (4.0 vs 3.0); Vercel is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0). 8.5 of the 10.9 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Thousands of users connected at once need processes that keep their connections open. Request-scoped functions either cannot hold a WebSocket (Lambda behind a function URL, Netlify) or hold each one as a running function pinned to one instance (Vercel beta), so broadcasting to all of them needs a separate pub/sub or realtime service.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 4.7 points. Fly.io is stronger on realtime fit (5.0 vs 4.0), team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5); AWS ECS on Fargate is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 3.0). 2.0 of the 4.7 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Anycast + multi-region VMs keep websocket round-trips short for global users.

tradeoffs: No free plan for new organizations (a trial of 2 machine-hours or 7 days); the smallest always-on machine costs about $2.19 a month

supporting.justification: Read-heavy traffic, a tight latency target or hot key-value data: keep hot reads and sessions in memory in front of a durable primary database. The 100 ms p95 target (requirements.p95_latency_ms) leaves little time for repeated database reads.

alternatives.choice: A CDN or HTTP cache in front of the API
alternatives.why_not: It caches whole public responses only, not sessions, counters or per-user data

alternatives.choice: The database's own buffer cache only
alternatives.why_not: It holds hot rows only until the working set outgrows the database's memory, and every read still costs a database round trip

tradeoffs: Cached data can be stale: each write must expire or update the keys it changes

supporting.choice: Redis pub/sub for cross-instance fan-out (Upstash Redis on Fly)
supporting.justification: With several app instances, a message published on one must reach sockets on all others. Up to 5,000 users online at once (scale.peak_concurrent_users) hold open connections.

alternatives.why_not: Server to client only; chat, presence and live edits need messages both ways

alternatives.choice: Polling the API every few seconds
alternatives.why_not: Every client asks again and again, which multiplies requests and still shows changes late

tradeoffs: Open connections hold memory per user and need pub/sub to reach users on other instances

supporting.choice: Yjs shared documents (CRDTs) synced over the WebSocket connection, with Hocuspocus as the sync server (a Node.js service beside the Go API)
supporting.justification: Many people editing one document at once need conflict-free merging; CRDTs merge concurrent edits without locks, and the server stores snapshots, not every stroke. Hocuspocus runs on Node.js, so it is a second runtime to deploy and monitor beside Go; the Go API keeps sign-in and permissions and Hocuspocus calls it to check each connection.

alternatives.choice: Locking the document while one person edits
alternatives.why_not: Only one person can edit at a time, which is not multi-user editing
A central server must order every edit, and offline edits merge less cleanly than with CRDTs

tradeoffs: Document snapshots grow with edit history and need compaction

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path.

alternatives.why_not: Fixed schedules only: no retries, no priorities and nothing started by a user's action

alternatives.choice: Doing the work inside the web request
alternatives.why_not: Slow emails, uploads and API calls would hold the request open and fail with it

tradeoffs: A job can run twice after a retry, so handlers must be idempotent

supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database. The scenario stores 200 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Files on the app server's disk
alternatives.why_not: Lost when an instance is replaced, and not shared between instances
They bloat backups and the database disk, which costs several times more per GB than object storage

tradeoffs: Files and their database rows can drift apart: delete or replace both together

supporting.choice: Cloudflare CDN in front of the uploads bucket
supporting.justification: Serve uploads from the CDN, not the app server; resize images on the fly instead of storing every size.

alternatives.choice: Public links to the object store
alternatives.why_not: No resizing or edge caching, and private files would be reachable by anyone with the link

alternatives.choice: Serving files through the app server
alternatives.why_not: Each download holds an app connection and pays the app host's egress price

tradeoffs: Links that leak can be shared until they expire, so keep their lifetime short

supporting.justification: Card data never touches your servers, which keeps your PCI-DSS audit scope to the smallest self-assessment form (SAQ A).

alternatives.why_not: Suits large merchants with negotiated contracts; more setup than a first release needs

alternatives.choice: Taking card details on your own pages
alternatives.why_not: Card data on your servers moves the PCI-DSS audit from the shortest self-assessment (SAQ A) to a full one

tradeoffs: Every transaction pays the gateway's fee, and refunds and disputes follow its process

supporting.justification: Social sign-in (Google, Apple, GitHub) needs OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect flows, account linking and token refresh, which a maintained sign-in product or framework library handles. Clerk is a US company, so under GDPR sign its data processing agreement with Standard Contractual Clauses (GDPR Chapter V).

alternatives.why_not: A server to run, patch and back up, for no feature this project needs
Password storage, MFA, resets and lockouts are easy to get wrong and are the first things attackers test

tradeoffs: Sign-in depends on the identity provider staying up; moving users off it later is a migration

supporting.justification: Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target. A 99.9% availability target (requirements.availability) allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, so failures must show within minutes.

alternatives.why_not: They show the app is down, not why
Without traces and metrics there is no way to see which call is slow or failing

tradeoffs: Telemetry volume is billed: sample traces and set log retention

supporting.justification: Every push runs the tests and deploys the same way; hosted runners mean no build server to operate. All 5 engineers (team.size) release through the same pipeline.

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent pipelines; one more tool to learn for no gain here

alternatives.choice: Deploying by hand from a developer's machine
alternatives.why_not: No test gate, and each release depends on one person's setup

tradeoffs: Pipeline minutes are metered on hosted runners

assumptions: Planning estimate from published price bands at your scale tier, each read where the project sits inside its tier, with the usage terms listed per line; excludes salaries, third-party SaaS (auth, email, payments fees) and egress spikes.
Scale tier: Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once)

Hosting: Fly.io: $375-845 (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) price band, from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 521 req/s at peak (2% of the way up the tier, log scale); x1.5 for 99.9% availability (redundant instances))

Database: PostgreSQL: $600-1,244 (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) database tier (~200 GB in 12 months), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 521 req/s at peak (2% of the way up the tier, log scale); upper end for ~200 GB of data: the band's top is priced for the largest data of the tier; x1.5 for 99.9% availability (standby/replicas))

Cache: Redis / Valkey: $200-568 (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) price band (the app's scale), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 521 req/s at peak (2% of the way up the tier, log scale))
Media delivery: $15-135 (~1,500 GB served a month (5 MB per active user a day) at $0.01-0.09/GB)
Authentication: $0-25 (Clerk's free Hobby plan holds up to 50,000 monthly users (~50,000 here); its Pro plan, $25/month, adds production features (https://clerk.com/pricing))

warnings.message: Budget below the top of the estimate. $1,190-$2,817/month against $1,500/month: the top (~3x today's load) and the middle are over, most of the rise in PostgreSQL and Fly.io. Raise the budget before the load grows.

Fly.io publishes no uptime SLA. Your 99.9% target rests on the app alone: Fly.io commits to no uptime figure and owes no credit when it is down. Alert on an external uptime check and keep a fallback ready (a second region or provider); pick a host with a published SLA if the target is contractual.

Card payments: the hosted checkout collects card numbers on the payment provider's page, so your PCI DSS check is the shortest self-assessment (SAQ A). Putting card fields on your own pages, or storing card numbers, widens the audit.

GDPR: sign a data processing agreement with every vendor that handles personal data, honour access and deletion requests, and report a breach within 72 hours; a vendor outside the EU needs Standard Contractual Clauses or the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.

assumptions: project.description sets no field in a scenario file: every choice comes from the structured fields, so wording cannot move the stack (in the app, the description reader only suggests fields for you to confirm); a fixed keyword list adds the 'Read from project.description' notes, which change no pick
Read from project.description ('per seat'): bill through the payment provider's subscriptions with the seat count as the quantity, updated when an organisation adds or removes members
Sized for scale.users_12_months: 50,000 users, about 10,000 active on a day (20% daily-to-monthly ratio); scale.users_at_launch (1,000) is the starting point
gdpr with no data_residency: the users are taken to be in the EU, so the stack is placed in an EU region; this is a preference, not a residency rule

gdpr: sign a data processing agreement (DPA) with every vendor that stores or processes personal data (host, database, sign-in, payments, monitoring); with no EU residency stated, personal data may leave the EU only under an adequacy decision or the vendor's Standard Contractual Clauses (GDPR Chapter V); set infrastructure.data_residency to eu to keep it in EU regions
Priorities rated 4 or 5 raise their criteria's weights, strongest first: scalability (5), performance (5), maintainability (4)
Priorities rated 1 or 2 (cost) keep their criteria at the baseline weight

Questionnaire answers the scenario schema has no field for took their defaults: data_shapes 'relational', consistency 'strong', architecture 'auto', lock_in_tolerance 'medium' (an extensions block can set them)
